cards.title: The Sunk-Cost Trap: Why Past Effort Shouldn’t Decide Your Next Move
cards.hook: The more time, money or pride you have invested, the harder it becomes to walk away—even when walking away is rational.
cards.lead: A sunk cost is a cost you cannot recover. Rationally, it should not affect what you do next. Psychologically, however, people often keep investing because stopping would make the earlier investment feel wasted.
sections: Imagine you have spent months building a product feature that users barely touch. The time is already gone. The useful question is not ‘How much have we invested?’ but ‘Given what we know now, where should the next hour or euro go?’ Only future costs and future benefits should drive the choice.

Stopping can feel like admitting failure, so we search for reasons to continue. This is intensified by loss aversion, ego and consistency pressure. The result is escalation of commitment: more resources are added mainly to justify what has already been spent.

Use a reset question: If I had not already invested anything, would I choose this option today? Another method is to define exit criteria in advance—for example, ‘If fewer than 15% of test users activate this feature after three iterations, we stop or redesign it.’ Pre-committed criteria make emotional rationalisation harder.
cards.takeaway: Do not ask whether previous effort deserves to be rescued. Ask which option creates the highest expected value from this point forward.
cards.q: Which question best protects against the sunk-cost fallacy?
options: How much have we already invested?
Would we choose this option today if we were starting from zero?
How can we justify our earlier decision?
Can we invest a little more so the previous effort was not wasted?
cards.prompt: Name one current commitment where a ‘start from zero today’ test could change your next decision.

cards.title: Build–Measure–Learn: The Core Loop of The Lean Startup
cards.hook: A startup should not ask ‘Can we build this?’ first. It should ask ‘What do we need to learn next?’
cards.lead: Eric Ries treats a startup as an experiment under extreme uncertainty. Progress is not simply shipping more features; it is learning, with evidence, what customers actually value.
sections: Every new venture rests on assumptions. Two especially important ones are the value hypothesis—whether the product creates enough value for customers—and the growth hypothesis—how adoption could spread. Instead of polishing a complete product first, identify the assumption that could kill the idea if it is wrong.
The MVP is a learning tool

A minimum viable product is the smallest experiment that can produce useful evidence about a key assumption. ‘Minimum’ does not mean careless or low quality. It means avoiding work that does not help answer the current question. Sometimes the MVP is software; sometimes it is a landing page, manual service, prototype or direct customer test.

After building the experiment, measure behaviour rather than relying only on compliments. Compare what happened with what you expected. If the evidence supports the underlying assumptions, improve and continue. If it repeatedly contradicts them, change an important part of the strategy—a pivot—while keeping what you have learned.
cards.takeaway: Build–Measure–Learn turns product development into a sequence of experiments: identify a risky assumption, test it cheaply, measure real behaviour and let the evidence shape the next move.
cards.q: What is the primary purpose of an MVP in Lean Startup thinking?
options: To launch the cheapest possible finished product
To impress investors with as many features as possible
To test a key assumption and generate validated learning
To avoid speaking with customers until the product is polished
cards.prompt: For one idea you are working on, state one risky assumption and the smallest experiment that could test it.
